The Eastern spinebill (Acanthorhynchus tenuirostris) is a small, active honeyeater that demonstrates a remarkably high metabolic rate for its size. When measured under standard thermoneutral conditions at a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the basal oxygen consumption of this species reaches approximately 49.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 49.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that underscores the energetic demands of its nectarivorous foraging lifestyle. This metabolic intensity is typical of meliphagids that engage in rapid, hovering flight while exploiting floral resources, and it aligns closely with predictions for birds of this body mass. The elevated metabolic expenditure is sustained by a diet rich in simple sugars, which are readily absorbed and oxidized to fuel the high wingbeat frequencies observed during feeding bouts. Comparative studies with other Australian honeyeaters indicate that the spinebill’s resting metabolism is among the more elevated for its body size class, reflecting an evolutionary adaptation to a high-throughput energy acquisition strategy.

Reproductive output in this species is modest, reflecting a life-history strategy geared toward extended parental investment rather than high fecundity. When maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with each clutch containing two to three eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing two to three eggs]. This low fecundity is offset by intensive biparental care and a prolonged nestling period, which together enhance the survival prospects of each offspring. The energetic cost of producing even a small clutch is substantial for a bird of this size, and the trade-off between current reproductive effort and future survival likely constrains females to a single breeding attempt per season. Field observations confirm that renesting following failure is uncommon, further emphasizing the conservative nature of the species’ reproductive strategy.

Neonates emerge at a remarkably small body mass, with newly hatched chicks weighing just 1.79 grams [Wwb = 1.79 grams]. This extremely low birth mass is characteristic of altricial passerines and places the hatchling in a state of complete dependence on parental provisioning for both warmth and nutrition. The incubation period, during which eggs are held at a developmental temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], after which the altricial young require an extended period of intensive brooding. The nestling phase is a critical window of rapid mass gain, during which the chick must achieve a several-fold increase in body size before it can fledge. This initial mass of less than two grams represents only a tiny fraction of the adult body mass, underscoring the profound developmental trajectory that must be completed within the nest. The energetic burden on the parents during this phase is substantial, as they must make frequent foraging trips to meet the growing chick’s metabolic demands.

The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate adult body mass, a pattern that likely reflects divergent selective pressures on males and females. Females attain a maximum adult body mass of 9.725 grams [Wwi = 9.725 grams], whereas males are substantially larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 11.25 grams [Wwi = 11.25 grams]. This degree of dimorphism is moderate compared to some other honeyeaters and may be linked to male-male competition for access to territories and floral resources. The larger body size of males likely confers an advantage in aggressive interactions over high-quality feeding patches, while the smaller female body size may reduce energetic costs during the demanding breeding season. Size differences are also reflected in subtle variations in bill morphology, with males possessing slightly longer, more curved bills that may allow access to different flower types. These mass differences are consistent across populations and appear to be a stable life-history trait of the species.

At 40 °C [T = 40 °C], fledging occurs at 31.5 days since birth [tx = 31.5 days since birth], marking the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest. Puberty, or the attainment of sexual maturity, follows considerably later at 180 days since birth [tp = 180 days since birth], a delay that allows young birds to refine foraging skills and establish their own territories at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. First reproduction, however, is deferred even further, with the first brood typically initiated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This pattern of postponed breeding is common among small passerines that require an extended period of learning and social integration. At 40 °C [T = 40 °C], maximum recorded longevity in the wild for the Eastern spinebill is approximately 15.5 years [am = approximately 15.5 years], a remarkably long lifespan for such a small bird and one that likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality associated with a relatively predator-safe, nectar-rich environment.
